about: Heat inside factories (November 2026): the evidence behind /factory-heat/. Occupational guidance (EU-OSHA, US OSHA and NIOSH, Canada's CCOHS, the ILO), one controlled trial of garment-work cooling in a climate chamber, field reports from operating apparel factories (Better Work, IFC, Cornell GLI, GIZ), a modelling study of fans and a review of cooling strategies. Each claim names the exact words its source must hold; a claim reaches the page only when every one was found. US and EU sources inform mechanisms and design; where they set legal duties, the page names the jurisdiction. Field reports are reports from operating factories, mostly by management or programme staff, not independent evaluations; the trial is a laboratory simulation, not a factory-wide field trial.

claims.text: EU-OSHA defines heat stress as the overall heat load from metabolic heat, clothing and the environment: air temperature and movement, humidity and radiant heat.
rests_on: metabolic heat, clothing, and environmental factors

claims.text: Mild or moderate heat stress can cause discomfort and affect performance and safety without harming health; extremes compromise the body's ability to regulate its temperature.
rests_on: Mild or moderate heat stress can lead to discomfort

claims.text: Radiant heat reaches the body from hot objects such as hot metal, furnaces and steam pipes without contact; the sun is a common source.
rests_on: hot metal, furnaces and steam pipes
common example of a source of radiant heat

claims.text: Indoor workers are also at risk of heat stress, especially in poorly cooled buildings.
rests_on: Indoor workers are also at risk of heat stress

claims.text: EU-OSHA's engineering controls include reducing heat release, reflective or heat-absorbing shielding, insulating or enclosing heat-generating processes or separating them from workers, and covering hot surfaces with low-emissivity material.
It lists reducing humidity by eliminating open hot water baths, drains and leaky steam valves, and removing heated air or steam from hot processes with local exhaust ventilation.
rests_on: removing heated air or steam from hot processes using local exhaust ventilation

claims.text: It lists shading workers from direct sunlight with blinds or reflective film on windows, and positioning workstations away from direct sunlight or sources of heat.
rests_on: positioning workstations away from direct sunlight

claims.text: It lists fans and air movement, particularly in humid conditions, without compromising local exhaust ventilation installed on machinery.
It lists air-conditioned, shaded or cool break areas as close as possible to the work site.
rests_on: as close as possible to the work site

claims.text: In very hot industrial areas, ventilation, localised air conditioning and cooled observation booths are commonly used to provide cool workstations.
The risk assessment needs revising regularly and when conditions change, and technical or organisational changes need checking so that they do not increase the risk for workers.
rests_on: do not increase the risk for workers

claims.text: EU-OSHA notes that the risk assessment already covers pregnant workers and may be reviewed when a worker says she is pregnant; in very hot work a pregnant woman's core temperature may rise.
On average about one litre of water an hour may be needed to replace sweat losses, and drinking every 15 to 20 minutes is encouraged: an average from guidance, not an individual prescription.
rests_on: about one litre of water every hour

claims.text: In the EU, the Workplaces Directive requires the temperature in rooms containing workstations to be adequate for human beings; most legislation sets no specific maximum, so national legislation needs checking.
US OSHA's engineering controls include reflective shields, insulation of hot surfaces, elimination of steam leaks, local exhaust ventilation and mechanical equipment to reduce manual work.
OSHA's Technical Manual describes WBGT as combining the natural wet bulb temperature, the globe temperature and, outdoors, the dry bulb temperature.
OSHA's Technical Manual distinguishes heat stress, the load on the body, from heat strain, the body's response to it.
NIOSH recommends acclimatisation for workers new to heat, beginning with no more than 20% of the usual duration of heat exposure on the first day.
NIOSH's criteria for a recommended standard on occupational exposure to heat and hot environments (2016) set out recommended exposure limits that depend on work intensity.
rests_on: Occupational Exposure to Heat and Hot Environments

claims.text: A randomised crossover trial in a climate chamber at the University of Sydney had 42 healthy participants aged 18 to 40 complete 3-hour garment-work simulations (men ironed, women sewed) at a control condition of 40 °C and 38% relative humidity, representing a non-air-conditioned Bangladeshi factory.

Compared with the control, men's core temperature fell with a fan plus drinking water, with a modified rooftop (37.5 °C) and with air conditioning (24 °C); women's core temperature fell only with air conditioning. Heart rate and sweat-loss fluid deficit fell with several of the alternatives in both groups.
rests_on: core temperature decreased only with AC

claims.text: The trial found cooling benefits were greater in men, which its authors read as a sign of possible gender-based inequalities in workplace heat stress.
rests_on: Cooling benefits were greater in males

claims.text: The ILO code of practice on safety and health in textiles, clothing, leather and footwear, adopted by experts from governments, employers and workers in October 2021, is the first for these industries and covers chemical, ergonomic and physical hazards, machinery and building and fire safety.

In an IFC case study at an apparel factory in Bangladesh, an uninsulated exhaust-gas boiler and pipes producing steam for the pressing section had surface temperatures above 100 °C; after insulation, the factory reported lower heat loss and energy use and improved indoor air temperature.

Factory management in Bangladesh reports that in the monsoon or on rainy days, added humidity makes fabric absorb moisture and affects product quality, so evaporative cooling does not suit every season.

A textile and apparel manufacturer in Pakistan combining exhaust fans, refrigerant air-cooling and evaporative air-conditioners reported average monthly indoor temperatures of 27 to 31 °C in the three hottest months of 2022.
A large apparel manufacturer in Cambodia combining evaporative cooling, exhaust fans, 13-metre ceilings and a roof heat shield reported dry-bulb temperatures below 32 °C.
Better Work staff found over half the factories visited in Egypt had workstation fans and 15% had evaporative cooling; in Nicaragua slightly more than a third had evaporative cooling.
Viet Nam's Ministry of Health sets WBGT limits that fall as work gets heavier and as the share of time exposed rises.

Bangladesh's Labour Act of 2006 requires adequate ventilation and comfortable temperatures; the 2015 Labour Rules call for at least one thermometer in every workroom, and the law does not specify temperatures or thresholds.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh excludes indoor heat from its remit.
rests_on: indoor heat is excluded from its remit

claims.text: The report proposes treating extreme climate events as force majeure in labour law and buyer agreements, with allowances in production schedules, delivery, leave and income, and treating heat stress as a health hazard with a right to stop work without penalty or loss of income.
rests_on: without penalty or loss of income

claims.text: The report asks for particular attention to pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers, for whom access to potable drinking water is critical, and for women workers' voices in production schedules, given unpaid care work.
Better Factories Cambodia's 32 °C threshold is a dry-bulb measurement, not WBGT, with readings typically taken between 12:00 and 14:00.
The report cites an estimated average fall of 1.5% in productivity for moderate effort in manufacturing for every 1 °C above 25 °C WBGT.
rests_on: productivity for moderate effort in manufacturing

claims.text: Across 800 Better Factories Cambodia assessments in the hottest months of 2015 to 2024, 82% of factories had hottest production areas above the programme's own 32 °C dry-bulb threshold, which is not set by law, and one in three had days above 35 °C.
Almost 53% of the factories were above 32 °C while also hotter than the concurrent outdoor temperature.
In Bangladesh, Better Work advisers reported workers turning off production floor lights to reduce the heat, creating a low-light problem.
rests_on: turned off their production floor lights

claims.text: An adviser in Viet Nam described management responding reactively to worker complaints of heat by setting up fans.
Workers know where heat accumulates, where airflow is weak, where equipment fails and where uniforms or production systems increase risk.

Low-cost measures such as water access, ventilation, fans, shaded rest areas, maintenance and adjusted breaks can be put in place quickly; roof insulation, evaporative cooling, water curtains, sensors and retrofits need capital, planning and buyer support.
rests_on: Low-cost measures such as water access

claims.text: In Cambodia, a possible revision of Prakas 147 on workplace thermal environments could add WBGT-based thresholds and work-rest protocols.
Pregnant workers and workers with long commutes or unpaid care responsibilities may have less time to rest, rehydrate and recover outside working hours.
Dry-bulb (air) temperature does not capture humidity, air movement or radiant heat, which heat stress indicators such as WBGT reflect more fully.
rests_on: does not capture humidity, air movement or radiant heat

claims.text: One Cambodian garment factory in Cornell GLI's case studies has 45 temperature and humidity sensors that workers and managers can see, and logs readings several times a day.

At that factory, workers report warm corners, stagnant air and discomfort near machines through their union and a messaging app, and cooling improvements formed part of the bargaining relationship with the union.

Evaporative pads (water curtains) pull outside air through water-saturated pads under negative pressure, cooling it by five to twelve degrees depending on humidity; at that factory they created uneven airflow, and workers nearest the vents wore light jackets.
rests_on: five to twelve degrees, depending on humidity

claims.text: At a factory in Viet Nam, management and technical staff reported that rooftop solar panels shading the roof, combined with new insulation, lowered indoor temperatures by around 3 °C.
Heat at home disrupts workers' sleep and recovery, and its effects carry into the production environment even in factories with effective indoor cooling.

Canada's CCOHS notes that extreme heat raises the risk of dehydration and heat exhaustion in pregnancy and can affect the fetus if core body temperature rises above 38 °C, and suggests tasks earlier in the day or in cooler places, with work-rest cycles.

The ILO Maternity Protection Convention, 2000 (No. 183) provides, in countries that ratify it, a right to one or more daily breaks or a daily reduction of hours to breastfeed, counted as working time and paid.

In India, the health ministry and UNFPA India published guidance on heat and pregnancy for healthcare providers and community health workers, with a heat-risk checklist and preparedness for health facilities including functional referral systems.

A 2021 Lancet review argues that reliance on air conditioning is unsustainable and further marginalises the communities most vulnerable to heat, and summarises the benefits and limits of cooling strategies for settings including workplaces.

A biophysical modelling study across 108 cities found electric fans would not have worsened heat stress for healthy young adults on most hot days, and proposed humidity-dependent temperature thresholds above which fans worsen heat stress; it modelled population groups, not factory tasks.
In garment factories near Bengaluru, a working paper found that switching to LED lighting, which gives off less heat, softened the drop in output on hot days.
In a survey of 753 women at three garment factories in Phnom Penh, the share reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months, by their own reports.
WHO and WMO issued a report and guidance in 2025 to protect workers from increasing heat stress.
